Michael M. Santiago | Getty Images Stocks were mixed on Friday as traders headed for a mostly losing week amid a rotation out of tech and artificial intelligence-related names. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 243 points, or 0.5%, while the Nasdaq Composite shed 0.5%. The S&P 500 traded around the flatline. Chipmakers were lower again. The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) lost 1%, led by declines in Micron Technology , Advanced Micro Devices and Sandisk . Semiconductors have struggled this week amid jitters about competition from China . The SMH is down 8% week to date. Those declines, coupled with drops in other stocks linked to AI, put the S&P 500 on pace for a losing week. The benchmark index is down almost 1% this week, while the Nasdaq has shed about 3%. The Dow, on the other hand, has moved higher by more than 1% on the week. Investors have also grown concerned that tech companies are borrowing too much for the AI buildout . Shares of neoclouds like CoreWeave , which has seen its debt and obligations rise to more than $51 billion , were down around 9%, putting the stock's week-to-date losses at more than 22%. "The question is: Is this a systemic issue?" said Michael Rosen, Angeles' chief investment officer. "Obviously, increased debt issuance is something to observe and continue to watch and be concerned about if it continues to get to levels of excessiveness. But we're not remotely close to that right now." Other areas of the market such as financials saw gains. JPMorgan and Goldman Sachs advanced around 2% and 1%, respectively. Additionally, shares of sporting goods retailer Nike and drugmaker Merck each climbed around 1%, adding to the Dow's rise. Simultaneously, investors have been grappling with hotter-than-expected inflation data, which has been exacerbated by elevated energy prices in the wake of the U.S.-Iran war. Wholesale inflation this week saw its biggest gain since 2022 , while consumer inflation remained well above the Federal Reserve's target of 2%. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh spoke at an IMF event in Bangkok overnight. And while he didn't comment on whether the Fed would raise rates before year-end, traders took that as a sign that the central bank will hold policy steady later this month. headlines.title: SpaceX AI policy leader grilled by NYC Council on Grok safety, sexualized images
headlines.summary: SpaceX head of global government affairs for AI Gabriela Castillo Madrid faced critical questions from the New York City Council on Friday.
headlines.article_text: SpaceX policy manger grilled by NYC Council on Grok AI safety, images Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points SpaceX head of global government affairs for AI Gabriela Castillo Madrid faced questions about Grok's generation of sexualized images from the New York City Council on Friday. NYC Council Speaker Julie Menin asked why she was able to pull up sexualized images of herself when Castillo Madrid said Grok does not let users create such images of real people. Elon Musk's aerospace and AI company previously evaded a subpoena to testify as part of a legislative investigation and hearing held last week. In this article SPCX Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT The SpaceX headquarters is seen on Monday, Aug. 3, 2026 in Hawthorne, CA. Eric Thayer | Los Angeles Times | Getty Images SpaceX artificial intelligence policy leader Gabriela Castillo Madrid faced a tough line of questioning from NYC Council Speaker Julie Menin on Friday as part of a legislative investigation into AI safety. When Castillo Madrid claimed that the company had appropriate "safeguards" in place around its AI products, Menin immediately confronted her. "I'm going to completely push back on that," Menin said. "I mean, just this morning — myself and my team — we put our own names, my own name, into Grok, and there's absolutely a sexualized image of myself. So then, how is it that within a second, I could find a sexualized image of myself using Grok?" Castillo Madrid responded that the company has "strict controls" and would have the safety team look into that specific instance. NYC Council Member Carmen De La Rosa, who leads the council's tech committee, told Castillo Madrid that "it is disgusting" that Grok enables users to easily "sexualize" images of real women without their consent. "I just don't understand how you can say that there are these safe models," Menin said. "It's just unacceptable." Castillo Madrid appeared in front of the council's tech committee by video. Elon Musk's aerospace, defense tech and AI company originally evaded requests and a subpoena from the city council to appear alongside leaders from OpenAI , Anthropic , Google and Meta on Oct. 5. SpaceX agreed to testify earlier this week after the council threatened to have its subpoena enforced by a judge. The council opened its probe following a month of intense debate surrounding the risks posed by advanced AI models, and is aiming to use testimony and information unearthed through the investigation to guide new regulations. Read more CNBC tech news Amazon launches new Bee 'personal AI' devices that listen to conversations Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang urges U.S.-China dialogue on 'potentially dangerous' AI OpenAI sued by 8 states over ChatGPT safety concerns Anthropic's third-quarter revenue is said to hit $16.8 billion ahead of IPO Before Castillo Madrid took a role in government affairs at SpaceX earlier this year, she worked at X, Musk's social media company that's now owned by SpaceX, according to her LinkedIn profile . Prior to that, she spent almost three years at the U.S. Department of Commerce. De La Rosa asked Castillo Madrid how many whistleblowers the company has fired, to which Castillo Madrid said she was "not aware" of any. "I just want to interject for a minute because Devin Kim, one of your former employees, was reportedly fired after he sounded the alarm about serious safety concerns," Menin said. "I'm not aware with that specific case," Castillo Madrid responded, adding that the company has a culture where "everybody has a an ability to say something when they see something." Kim is now President of the nonprofit Center for AI Safety, a think tank focused on AI risks and safety. The council further pressed Castillo Madrid about the misuse of Grok and the types of safeguards that are in place. Councilmember Mercedes Narcisse asked why the company promoted the idea of users uploading X-rays to Grok, asking if that was safe and if HIPPA protections applied. SpaceX's Castillo Madrid said Grok is "not meant to be a clinician, a doctor," adding, "in terms of privacy, users decide whether their Grok conversations are used to train our models or not." Narcisse said it was dangerous to tell people "openly on X, to put their MRI, X-rays," into Grok and expect "a definite answer" on health matters. The council member then upbraided the SpaceX representative for the vagueness of some of her replies. "You're supposed to give us answers, you're not," she said. In merging SpaceX with xAI in February, Musk combined his AI and social networking business with his rocket launch company, which also owns the Starlink satellite internet service. The merger put SpaceX in control of AI model Grok, which is used by some federal agencies, including the Pentagon . SpaceX went public in June and is now valued at about $2 trillion. In August, SpaceX completed a $60 billion acquisition of AI coding startup Cursor. In skipping the earlier NYC Council hearing, SpaceX avoided direct questioning from a member of the U.K. Parliament, Jess Asato, who testified about experiencing AI-enabled online harassment. Asato is suing xAI in the U.K. after Grok users created and distributed sexualized images of her online without her consent. She's seeking damages, alleging misuse of her private information and breaches of European data protection rules. According to the BBC , Asato criticized SpaceX for its "arrogance" in not appearing last week. SpaceX didn't respond to a request for comment ahead of the meeting. Photographer: /Bloomberg via Getty Images Zed Jameson | Bloomberg via Getty Images Shares of French Satellite Group Eutelsat soared this week as SpaceX 's Starshield drew criticism after the Ukrainian military's access to its systems was suddenly restricted. Earlier this week, tensions rose between the U.S. and Ukraine after Kyiv accused Elon Musk's SpaceX of imposing new restrictions on its military-grade Starlink internet service without warning, curbing connectivity and limiting Ukraine's ability to defend itself against Russian attacks. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy criticized the U.S., saying "Starlink was switched off" in the middle of the night, preventing Ukrainian drones from intercepting Russian attacks, and ultimately contributing to civilian deaths. "They knew what they did," Zelenskyy said. "It's not about attack. It's also about defending the lives… People were killed because not enough destroying, not enough interceptors, including interceptors with Starlink, which didn't work." SpaceX CEO Elon Musk responded by shifting blame on the U.S. government and said that Starshield systems were under Washington and President Donald Trump's control. Eutelsat shares rose 19% on Friday, and was up 25% over the past five days following the news of Starlink's struggles in Ukraine. Eutelsat shares over the past five days. Eutelsat's share move this week is more evidence "supporting the sovereign value of European Satellite networks," Deutsche Bank analysts said in a note Thursday. Markets viewed Eutelsat as "the credible Starlink alternative" amid the disruption, they added. "Whilst we note Eutelsat does offer a global LEO [Low Earth Orbit] constellation, we believe it lacks the scale to offer the number of terminals that Starlink can provide," they added. "We would expect the shares to give up some of the gains." Eutelsat consolidated with satellite internet provider OneWeb in 2023, looking to challenge Starlink's market dominance. However, Eutelsat currently has over 600 satellites in orbit, while Starlink has more than 6,750, the company's websites show. Ukraine's deputy minister for recovery, infrastructure, and transport Serhiy Derkach told CNBC on Friday that Russia had amped up attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure, taking advantage of restrictions on military applications, including striking bridges, railway networks, and border crossings. "With U.S. limiting the use of Starlinks on the battlefield, Russia feels that this is their moment to try and inflict even more pain and suffering on Ukraine's civilian infrastructure," Derkach said. "We are definitely moving towards very harsh weeks and months and need our partners' support now more than ever," he said, adding that Ukrainians already experience blackouts lasting 4-12 hours per day. headlines.summary: Elon Musk first debuted the Roadster refresh concept in 2017 but Tesla has since missed every targeted delivery date.
headlines.article_text: Tesla Roadster reveal: What to know about the delayed EV Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Tesla revealed its next-generation Roadster from a SpaceX test site in Texas on Thursday. CEO Elon Musk first debuted the Roadster refresh concept in 2017 but Tesla has since missed every targeted delivery date. Tesla said the new Roadster, equipped with SpaceX thrusters, can accelerate from zero to 60 miles per hour in less than a second. In this article TSLA SPCX Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 8:08 08:08 Tesla unveils long-delayed Roadster, showing off its flying-car ambitions Squawk Box Tesla showed off its long-delayed next-generation Roadster on Thursday, almost a decade after Elon Musk's company started taking deposits for the electric sports car. The event was livestreamed from a SpaceX test site in McGregor, Texas, near Waco, starting at 7:55 p.m. local time, or 8:55 p.m. ET. In attendance along with Musk were design leader Franz von Holzhausen and Lars Moravy, vice president of vehicle engineering. "You're going to see some crazy stuff tonight," Musk said. "You're going to see the results of what happens when you have a collaboration with the world's best car company and the world's best rocket company." Tesla's original Roadster, designed and engineered by a team led by founding CEO Martin Eberhard, was based on a Lotus Elise chassis and was first delivered in 2008, selling for roughly $100,000 in small volumes until 2012. Tesla unveils its long-delayed Roadster nearly a decade after first revealing a next-generation version of its original electric sports ​car, at a launch event in Waco, Texas, US, on October 15, 2026, in this still image taken from a handout video. Tesla | Via Reuters The next-generation Roadster is expected to be a high-end, low-volume model that relies on SpaceX technology to enable it to hover. While Musk fanatics expressed their excitement on social media, the Roadster isn't likely to have any material financial impact on the company. At the event, Musk and his team showcased a white sports car that raced up a curved ramp, then clung to it upside down and vaulted off it, flipping in mid-air and hovering slowly before landing on the ground. The two-seater can go from zero to 60 miles per hour in under a second, according to Tesla's timer, a feat Moravy demonstrated for the live audience. Musk said the next-generation Roadster would enter production in 2028. The price wasn't announced, and the company didn't disclose specifications about other performance-level variants of the new Roadster. It was unclear whether the vehicle would be street-legal, with Musk saying on stage that "This is not necessarily a safety-optimized car." The Roadster unveiling has added to speculation of a possible merger between Tesla and SpaceX. For years, Musk's companies have worked with and paid each other, even sharing some personnel. The collaboration has increased in 2026, with speculation about a possible SpaceX-Tesla merger swirling since the aerospace and defense company went public in June. SpaceX COO Gwynne Shotwell told CNBC ahead of the IPO that a merger "might make Elon's life a little easier." Barclays analyst Dan Levy predicted in a note out this week that such a merger could happen before the end of 2026. Tesla unveils its long-delayed Roadster nearly a decade after first revealing a next-generation version of its original electric sports ​car, at a launch event in Waco, Texas, US, on October 15, 2026 Source: Tesla Tesla reopened reservations for the refreshed Roadster in recent weeks, accepting $50,000 deposits from prospective buyers in the U.S., Canada and China. Musk first promoted the refreshed Roadster concept at an event in November 2017 , and the following June in a series of tweets. He wrote at that time, "SpaceX option package for new Tesla Roadster will include ~10 small rocket thrusters arranged seamlessly around car." The engines would improve speed and braking, and may "even allow a Tesla to fly." The prototype Tesla showed on Thursday is built to be as lightweight as possible with a steer-by-wire system, steering yoke, and an array of technologies developed by SpaceX, including thrusters, carbon overlay pressure vessels and diffusers, and powerful fans that enable the car to do some gymnastics. One feature Tesla left out of its forthcoming Roadster is the company's "FSD" or automated driving system. Musk said the new Roadster will be the last vehicle the company produces that's intended to be controlled by a human driver. Tesla started taking $50,000 deposits for the revamped Roadster in 2017, but has since missed every targeted delivery date. As recently as last October, Musk was hyping a Roadster demo that he hoped would happen before the end of 2025. That didn't take place either. Tesla unveils its long-delayed Roadster nearly a decade after first revealing a next-generation version of its original electric sports ​car, at a launch event in Waco, Texas, US, on October 15, 2026 Source: Tesla Musk's former friend and OpenAI co-founder Sam Altman mocked the Tesla CEO in posts on X last year over the extreme delays, showing screenshots of his reservation and refund requests. "I really was excited for the car! And I understand delays," Altman wrote. "But 7.5 years has felt like a long time to wait." Altman got his refund, and the two ended up in court earlier this year over a separate matter related to OpenAI's governance and ownership structure. Others have kept their reservations. Lawrence O'Connor, founder and CEO of Other World Computing in Austin, Texas, told CNBC ahead of the event that he reserved a Founder's Edition of the new Roadster in November 2017, effectively giving the company what he called an "interest-free loan" of $250,000. O'Connor wrote in a message that he would be attending the show and was "excited to see what has been 9 years in the making." After the event, O'Connor said what he saw was "off the charts." Tesla is scheduled to report third-quarter results after the bell on Wednesday.
